_about: Candidate answers / designs for quantitative problems in evolution, organism-design, development and morphology-and-scaling (problems.json). origin = 'proposed-here' (written in this run, not literature), 'source' (drawn from the cited source), or 'source-hypothesis+formalized-here' (hypothesis from the source; the quantitative condition was added here). checkable_against names which of the listed constraints could rule on the candidate; [] means none could. Constraints were NOT applied. uses_illustrative_values marks numbers chosen here only to make a candidate concrete.

constraints.square-cube: Square-cube scaling: under isometric growth by linear factor k, mass ~ k^3 while cross-sectional area and strength ~ k^2 (Galileo / Thompson).
constraints.kimura-neutral-rate: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate, independent of population size (Kimura).
constraints.neutral-fixation-probability: Neutral fixation probability is i/M for i copies among M; with selection not opposing the mutant, at least i/M (Kimura, extended).
constraints.neutral-substitution-budget: Neutral substitution budget over time T is mu*T per site.
constraints.fisher-fundamental-theorem-haploid: Fisher's fundamental theorem, haploid partial-change form: the change in mean fitness due to natural selection equals the additive genetic variance in fitness divided by mean fitness.
constraints.twofold-cost-of-sex: Maynard Smith's twofold cost of sex: at equal fecundity an asexual lineage grows twice as fast as a sexual one.
constraints.blueprint-well-formedness: Blueprint well-formedness: a part-of hierarchy must be acyclic, rooted, and taxon-consistent.

candidates.statement: Sex originated in isogamous unicells without separate males: every sexual individual is itself a fecund parent, so at equal per-individual fecundity the asexual:sexual per-generation growth ratio was 1, not 2.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The twofold-cost constraint states the growth ratio is 2 when sexual lineages spend half their offspring on males at equal fecundity; it decides whether that premise is absent here (ratio 1) or present (ratio 2).

candidates.statement: Sex originated in an anisogamous population (half of offspring male) and was favoured from the first generation because each sexual offspring had relative fitness (1+s) with s >= 1 over an asexual offspring.

commits_to.quantity: required per-offspring advantage of sexual offspring

candidates.checkable_rationale: With equal fecundity the asexual lineage grows twice as fast; the candidate survives only if (1+s) >= 2.

candidates.statement: Red Queen: parasites track common asexual clones, so common clones become disproportionately infected and are replaced by initially rare clones, periodically favouring genetically diverse sexuals (source). Quantitative form added here: sexuals persist if the time-averaged (geometric-mean) relative fitness of asexuals, after parasite-induced reduction, is <= 1/2 of its parasite-free value.

commits_to.quantity: required geometric-mean parasite-induced fitness reduction of asexuals (added here)

candidates.checkable_rationale: The factor 1/2 is exactly the offset needed against the twofold growth advantage at equal fecundity.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: The Maintenance of Sex, Clonal Dynamics, and Host-Parasite Coevolution in a Mixed Population of Sexual and Asexual Snails

candidates.statement: Lineage selection: within populations asexuals win (short-term twofold disadvantage of sex conceded), but asexual lineages have higher extinction rates, so sex is maintained at the level of lineages (source). Quantitative form added here: with asexual lineages arising at rate tau per sexual lineage and going extinct at rate e_a, sexual lineages persist at a non-zero share only if e_a exceeds e_s + tau.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The constraint fixes the within-population term the lineage-level argument must overcome; it cannot rule on the extinction-rate inequality itself.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Lineage Selection and the Maintenance of Sex

candidates.statement: Asexual females arising in sexual populations have at most half the fecundity of sexual females (developmental costs of parthenogenesis), so the twofold advantage never materialises.

commits_to.quantity: fecundity of asexual relative to sexual females

candidates.checkable_rationale: The constraint's premise is equal fecundity; it decides that the twofold advantage holds unless fecundity differs, which is exactly what this candidate claims (so it checks the premise, not the conclusion).

candidates.statement: The <1% share of asexual animal and seed-plant species (source figure) is explained if asexual lineages, despite growing twice as fast at equal fecundity, go extinct within a mean lifetime L_a <= L_s/10 of sexual lineages.

commits_to.value: <1% animals and seed plants; 10% ferns; ~20% fungi

candidates.checkable_rationale: The twofold cost supplies the short-term growth advantage the extinction term must override; the lifetime ratio itself is not decided by any listed constraint.

candidates.statement: Size at division follows a fixed added volume per cycle: V_div = V_birth + Delta, independent of V_birth; at steady state with symmetric division V_birth = Delta.
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns cell-cycle control.
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: Division is triggered by surface-to-volume limitation: a spherical cell growing isometrically has transport capacity ~ r^2 and demand ~ r^3, so it divides when r reaches r* = 3*J/q (J: area-specific uptake flux, q: volume-specific demand).
candidates.checkable_rationale: Isometric growth with area ~ L^2 vs volume ~ L^3 is exactly the square-cube premise.

candidates.statement: Growth stops when self-weight stress reaches tissue strength sigma*: for an organ growing isometrically, weight ~ L^3 over supporting section ~ L^2 gives stress ~ L, so L_final = sigma* / (c * rho * g) for a shape constant c.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Square-cube scaling gives the stress ~ L dependence the candidate relies on.

candidates.statement: Final organ size is set by a fixed cell count N* at constant cell volume v: organ volume = N* v; left/right size mismatch has relative SD ~ 1/sqrt(N*) if cell number is Poisson-distributed.
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns counting mechanisms.

candidates.statement: Developmental timing is set by counting n cycles of an oscillator with period P: stage onset time = n P; under a temperature change that scales P by factor f, all stage times scale by f.

commits_to.value: all stage times scale by the same factor f

candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns oscillators.

candidates.statement: Scaling a mouse heart to an elephant isometrically (linear factor k): heart mass ~ k^3 tracks body mass, but aortic cross-section ~ k^2, so cross-section per unit body mass falls as 1/k; the heart 'fits the rib cage' at all sizes only because both scale isometrically.

commits_to.quantity: aortic cross-section per unit body mass

candidates.checkable_rationale: Direct square-cube consequence under isometry.

candidates.statement: Left and right legs end up equal because each limb grows to a common circulating-signal threshold rather than counting its own cells; predicted left-right length difference is independent of limb cell number.

commits_to.quantity: dependence of left-right difference on cell number

candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns endocrine control.

candidates.statement: A limb scaled isometrically by k with unchanged proportions: bone cross-section ~ k^2, supported mass ~ k^3, peak bone stress during stance ~ k; selection on length alone at fixed proportions therefore raises stress linearly with length.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Isometric premise; stress = mass/area.

candidates.statement: Puberty begins when body mass first reaches a threshold M*: onset age t* solves M(t*) = M*; for linear growth M(t) = M0 + g t, t* = (M* - M0)/g, so onset age is inversely proportional to growth rate g.
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns endocrine triggers.
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: A 10 cm Arctic willow scaled isometrically to a 100 m tree (k = 1000; source gives 'barely 10 centimeters'): stem cross-section x 1e6, mass x 1e9, compressive stress at the base x 1000; without a change in shape or material, height is capped by stem strength.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Square-cube under isometry.

candidates.statement: Plant height is capped hydraulically: lifting water to height h needs tension >= rho g h plus flow losses, so h_max < P_cav/(rho g); for an assumed cavitation threshold P_cav = 10 MPa the hydrostatic-only bound is ~1000 m, so the observed maxima need flow-resistance limits.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Hydraulics are not among the listed constraints.

candidates.statement: A 10 t sauropod scaled isometrically to the source's 100 t: k = 10^(1/3) = 2.154; limb-bone cross-section x 4.64; bone stress x 2.154, unless limb bones became relatively thicker (positive allometry).
candidates.checkable_rationale: Direct square-cube prediction under isometry.

candidates.statement: Sauropod gigantism was made possible by a combination of plesiomorphic characters and key innovations, most importantly the very long neck (larger feeding envelope, more energy uptake), enabled by a small head and extensive pneumatization of the axial skeleton.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Feeding-envelope arguments are not decided by any listed constraint.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Biology of the sauropod dinosaurs: the evolution of gigantism

candidates.statement: Reaching 100 t in 20 years (source figures) requires a mean growth rate of 5 t/yr = 13.7 kg/day averaged over the growth period.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Arithmetic consequence; no listed constraint applies.

candidates.statement: The most important enabling circumstance for gigantism is a highly developed ecological infrastructure in which essential resources are abundant and effectively recycled; global giants are all aerobically active; gigantism appeared tens to hundreds of millions of years after mass extinctions.
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns ecological infrastructure.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Gigantism and Its Implications for the History of Life

candidates.statement: Maximum size of an aerobically active animal is set by surface-limited gas exchange: under isometry exchange area ~ L^2 and demand ~ L^3, so maximal size scales with the ratio of area-specific exchange capacity to mass-specific demand, and only lineages that break isometry of the exchange surface (folded lungs, gills) reach global-giant sizes.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Square-cube under isometry.

candidates.statement: Oxygen limitation via leg tracheae: tracheal volume scales with mass^1.29; tracheal cross-section through the leg orifice scales with mass^1.02 while the orifice scales with mass^0.77, so tracheae eventually fill the orifice and limit beetle size; hyperoxia shrinks required tracheae and raises that limit.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The source's exponents are empirical and non-isometric (0.77, not 2/3), so square-cube does not apply to the candidate as stated.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Increase in tracheal investment with beetle size supports hypothesis of oxygen limitation on insect gigantism

candidates.statement: An extant dragonfly of wingspan w0 scaled isometrically by k to a 1 m wingspan with unchanged leg and thorax proportions: leg cross-section and leg-orifice area ~ k^2, body mass ~ k^3, leg stress ~ k, tracheal diffusion path length ~ k; for w0 = 0.1 m (illustrative), k = 10: mass x 1000, orifice area x 100, leg stress x 10.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Isometric by construction.

candidates.statement: Denser hyperoxic air does not explain griffenfly gigantism: under isometry it would reduce hovering induced power by only 11% (a flyer 3% larger); with high-O2 power availability the largest hovering flyer would be only 1.19x longer than extant dragonflies (1.22x with allometry). Alternative: flight-muscle mass-specific power scaling (mass^0.24 in extant dragonflies) may have sufficed.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The source's main figures assume isometry; square-cube can check the isometric scaling steps.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Induced Power Scaling Alone Cannot Explain Griffenfly Gigantism.

candidates.statement: A leaf scaled isometrically by k: blade area ~ k^2, blade mass ~ k^3 (thickness scales too), petiole cross-section ~ k^2; petiole bending stress ~ (mass x lever arm)/section modulus ~ k^4/k^3 = k; the upper limit is where this stress reaches petiole strength.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Isometric mass vs cross-section scaling.

candidates.statement: Leaf width is limited by boundary-layer heat exchange: convective conductance per unit area ~ (wind speed / leaf width)^0.5 (laminar flat plate), so a leaf 10x wider has ~0.32x the conductance and overheats at equal irradiance; the upper limit is where leaf-air temperature excess reaches a lethal Delta_T_max.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Boundary-layer physics is not square-cube scaling.

candidates.statement: Asymmetric branching can be incorporated into the WBE model, and the 3/4 metabolic scaling exponent of Kleiber's law can still be attained within many asymmetric networks.
candidates.checkable_rationale: WBE network geometry is not among the listed constraints.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: A general model for metabolic scaling in self-similar asymmetric networks.

candidates.statement: Null: metabolism is limited by an exchange surface of an isometrically scaled body, so B ~ M^(2/3) (exponent 0.667), not 3/4.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Area ~ L^2 = M^(2/3) under isometry.

candidates.statement: Scaling mismatch between hydrodynamic accelerational forces and organism strength does not explain size limits; mechanisms combining the allometry of drag and strength accurately predict the maximal size of intertidal algae but not of animals; internally imposed inertial forces may limit large kelps.

commits_to.value: drag x strength allometry: algae yes, animals no

candidates.checkable_rationale: The source's argument uses empirical allometries, not isometry.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Are there mechanical limits to size in wave-swept organisms?

candidates.statement: Under isometry drag ~ L^2 u^2 and attachment strength ~ L^2, so drag stress is independent of size and drag alone sets no size limit; the acceleration reaction ~ L^3 du/dt gives stress ~ L, which does set a limit L_max proportional to strength/(rho du/dt).
candidates.checkable_rationale: Area vs volume scaling under isometry.

candidates.statement: Flight performance is power-limited: flight performance and total aerodynamic power scale with negative allometry; muscle strain and muscle stress increase with size, and longer wingbeat cycles may partially compensate for the constraint imposed by falling wingbeat frequency.

commits_to.quantity: allometry of performance and aerodynamic power (source)

candidates.checkable_rationale: The source's result is empirical; no listed constraint fixes it.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: The allometry of bird flight performance

candidates.statement: An isometrically scaled bird: wing area ~ L^2, mass ~ L^3, wing loading ~ L = M^(1/3), minimum flight speed ~ M^(1/6); if muscle mass-specific power is constant, the excess-power margin shrinks with size.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Isometric area vs mass.

candidates.statement: All crown animal phyla diverged within a window of T_w = 20 Myr; under neutrality the pairwise per-site divergence accumulated within the window is 2 mu T_w (0.04 for mu = 1e-9 per site per year), so inter-phylum molecular distances must be dominated by the time since the window.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate = mu and budget mu*T per lineage directly fix the expected divergence.

candidates.statement: The phyla diverged ~100 Myr before their first fossils (cryptic deep origin); expected neutral per-site divergence between two phyla is then 2 mu (T_fossil + 100 Myr), exceeding the fossil-only expectation by 2 mu x 100 Myr (0.2 at mu = 1e-9).
candidates.checkable_rationale: As above.

candidates.statement: Crown angiosperms originated Delta >= 50 Myr before the earliest unequivocal flower fossils; neutral sites accumulate mu x Delta substitutions per site along the stem in that interval, which must appear as excess crown-age branch length.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Budget mu*T.

candidates.statement: Neutral background: since the human-chimpanzee split T generations ago, expected neutral differences per site are 2 mu T (0.6% for mu = 1e-8 per site per generation, T = 3e5 generations); the human-specific changes of interest are a small subset of fewer than 100 positively selected regulatory changes against this background.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The background term is fixed by the neutral rate and budget; the count of selected changes is not.

candidates.statement: The 133 billion vs 400 million base difference (source figures) accrued by neutral insertions: the net substitution rate of insertions equals the insertion mutation rate, independent of population size, so over T = 400 Myr the lungfish lineage needed ~(133e9 - 0.4e9)/4e8 = 330 bp of net neutral insertion fixed per year.

commits_to.value: ~330 bp per genome per year over 400 Myr

candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate = mutation rate (no N dependence) and budget over T.

candidates.statement: Mutational hazard: extra DNA is slightly deleterious, so genomes expand only where effective population size is small enough that drift overwhelms selection (s < 1/(2N_e)).
candidates.checkable_rationale: The listed neutral constraints do not cover slightly deleterious variants (selection opposes).
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: Genome size was homogeneous across Paleozoic crown-tetrapod lineages (average haploid 2.9-3.7 pg), similar to extant mammals; expansion in amphibians, contraction along the diapsid lineage, and no directional change on the synapsid lineage, all in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Inferred from osteocyte-lacuna size; no listed constraint decides it.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Paleogenomic data suggest mammal-like genome size in the ancestral amniote and derived large genome size in amphibians.

candidates.statement: Longevity hypothesis: natural selection lowers the mitochondrial mutation rate in long-lived species; the substitution rate at cytochrome b third codon positions (taken as a mutation-rate proxy) varies 2 orders of magnitude, renewed every 1-2 Myr in the fastest mammals and >100 Myr in the slowest.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Reading synonymous substitution rate as mutation rate is exactly the neutral rate = mutation rate equivalence.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Strong Variations of Mitochondrial Mutation Rate across Mammals--the Longevity Hypothesis

candidates.statement: The ~100-fold variation in mitochondrial synonymous substitution rate is caused by differences in effective population size between lineages.
candidates.checkable_rationale: If synonymous sites are neutral, their substitution rate is independent of population size, so this candidate fails for neutral sites.

candidates.statement: Most laterally transferred genes are neutral in the recipient: they are fixed at a rate equal to the per-genome transfer rate, independent of population size, and a transfer present in i of M genomes fixes with probability i/M.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Kimura rate and fixation probability applied to transfer events as mutations.

candidates.statement: Retained transfers are on average beneficial (s > 0), so each has fixation probability at least i/M and the retained set is enriched relative to neutral expectation.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The extended lower bound applies when selection does not oppose.

candidates.statement: Bacterial ORFans originate by horizontal transfer, by rapid divergence from pre-existing genes, or by de novo emergence from noncoding sequence (the three hypotheses the source assesses; it concludes none is established).
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint partitions gene origins.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: De novo gene birth and the conundrum of ORFan genes in bacteria.

candidates.statement: A chirality-reversing mutation is neutral: reversed lineages arise at the mutation rate and each fixes with probability 1/M, so the rate of chiral reversal per lineage equals the reversal mutation rate.

commits_to.quantity: fixation probability of a new reversed mutant

candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate and fixation probability.

candidates.statement: Antisymmetry is rare because a population with chirality frequencies p and 1-p loses mating compatibility in a fraction ~2p(1-p) of encounters, so mixed states are unstable and a population moves to fixation of one chirality.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Selection opposes the minority chirality here, so the neutral bounds do not decide this candidate.

candidates.statement: Body plans are conserved not because the relevant mutations are rare (mutations duplicating body parts or changing the number of cervical vertebrae occur surprisingly frequently) but because strong interactivity during axial patterning makes them highly pleiotropic, with strong selection against them; relaxed selection temporarily lets novelties persist.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Selection opposes the mutants, so the neutral constraints give no bound.

source.name: abstract returned by `orx discover`
source.paper_title: Evolutionary novelties: the making and breaking of pleiotropic constraints

candidates.statement: Neutral null: if changes in cervical-vertebra number were neutral with per-generation mutation rate u, they would be substituted at rate u per lineage, and over G generations a lineage would accumulate u G count changes; observed conservation (u G << 1 changes) then requires either u < 1/G or rejection of neutrality.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate = mutation rate and budget over time.
candidates.notes: The conserved count (seven in most mammals) is not stated in the fetched abstract.

candidates.statement: Blood-group (e.g. ABO) alleles are old, maintained by balancing selection long enough to be shared across species that diverged before the human-chimpanzee split.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Balancing selection is outside the listed neutral constraints.
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: Blood-group allele frequencies are neutral: the probability that a given allele eventually fixes equals its current frequency (i/M), and the polymorphism is transient.

commits_to.quantity: fixation probability of an allele at frequency x

candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral fixation probability i/M.

candidates.statement: The heritable component is neutral overall: the alleles involved have no net fitness effect across carriers, so each fixes with probability equal to its frequency and is substituted at its mutation rate.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate and fixation probability apply if the net effect is zero.

candidates.statement: Sexually antagonistic selection: alleles that lower reproduction in carriers of one sex raise it in the other by enough that their average effect across sexes is >= 0, keeping a stable intermediate frequency.
candidates.checkable_rationale: The listed constraints do not decide whether a stable polymorphism exists.
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: Bet-hedging: a genotype producing phenotypic variance V_e among its clones has higher geometric-mean fitness across fluctuating environments than a fixed-phenotype genotype.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Not decided by the listed constraints.
candidates.notes: A hypothesis of this general form exists in the literature, but no source for it was fetched in this run, so it is labelled proposed-here and carries no citation.

candidates.statement: Intragenotypic variance persists because selection on that variance itself raises mean fitness each generation.

commits_to.quantity: additive genetic variance in fitness from intragenotypic differences

candidates.checkable_rationale: In the haploid partial-change form the change in mean fitness from selection is V_A(w)/mean(w); with V_A = 0 for this component it is 0, which rules out the candidate as stated.

candidates.statement: Additive variance V_A = sum_i 2 p_i q_i a_i^2; the unexplained part is carried by loci whose effects a_i fall below the detection threshold of genome-wide association studies, not by non-additive effects.
candidates.checkable_rationale: No listed constraint concerns detection power.

candidates.statement: If the loci affecting a trait are neutral, their between-species substitution rate equals their locus-specific mutation rate, so locus mutation rate, within-species polymorphism and between-species substitution rate must covary across loci (the pattern the source reports in Arabidopsis thaliana).
candidates.checkable_rationale: Neutral rate = mutation rate.

candidates.statement: Differences in mutational variance, and hence evolvability, arise from locus-specific mutation rates, mutational effect sizes, or mutational target size (number of loci); each has empirical support and they may contribute non-exclusively.

commits_to.value: mutation rate; effect size; target size

candidates.checkable_rationale: The source's partition is not decided by any listed constraint.

candidates.statement: With G the additive covariance matrix and unit selection direction b, unconditional evolvability e(b) = b'Gb and conditional evolvability c(b) = 1/(b'G^-1 b) satisfy c(b) <= e(b), with equality iff b is an eigenvector of G; pleiotropy reduces evolvability exactly by the ratio c/e.

candidates.statement: Plasticity-first: plastic traits produce variants that raise fitness and allow persistence until genetic accommodation, so more plastic traits evolve faster (the source calls this controversial and hard to test).

candidates.statement: Stasis occurs because additive genetic variance in fitness is zero over the stasis interval.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Fisher's partial change is V_A(w)/mean(w); the candidate claims it is 0, which the theorem links one-to-one to V_A(w) = 0; any measured V_A(w) > 0 refutes it.

candidates.statement: Much of the apparent year-to-year fluctuation in selection is sampling noise: true temporal variance of selection gradients = observed variance minus the mean squared standard error.
candidates.checkable_rationale: Statistical correction, not among listed constraints.
candidates.notes: Formalizes the source's remark that some estimates are inflated by sampling variance; the formula is added here.

candidates.statement: Low evolvability raises extinction rates: e.g. self-compatibility in species with bisexual flowers lowers evolvability and raises extinction rates in Solanaceae; the scattered phylogenetic distribution of asexual taxa reflects elevated extinction from low evolvability.
candidates.checkable_rationale: For the asexual case, the twofold short-term growth advantage of asexuals is what the elevated extinction must outweigh.

candidates.statement: Frame Shift Hypothesis: avian wing digits occupy positions 2, 3, 4 but carry developmental identities I, II, III, so identity shifted relative to position during theropod-bird evolution.
candidates.checkable_rationale: A digit part-of map must be taxon-consistent: a homology scheme that puts identity I at position 1 in non-avian theropods and position 2 in birds must declare the shift on a single branch, or the hierarchy is inconsistent.
